summary: Nicaragua sorts every nationality into three categories: Category A passports — most of Europe and the Americas plus Japan, Korea, Australia and the Gulf — need no visa and simply buy a USD 10 tourist card on arrival for up to 90 days, Category B nationalities apply for a consular visa, and Category C nationalities need a "consulted" visa approved in advance by immigration in Managua. Citizens of El Salvador, Guatemala and Honduras move freely under the CA-4 agreement.

conditionalWaivers.text: Travelers holding a valid US, Canadian or Schengen visa (class B2 or higher, valid at least six more months and already used at least once) are generally exempt from the Nicaraguan consular visa and buy the tourist card on arrival instead. The exemption does not apply to nationalities in Nicaragua's restricted category, which always require prior approval.

vaccinations.text: A yellow fever certificate is required if you are arriving from, or have recently transited, a country with risk of yellow fever transmission — which includes much of South America and sub-Saharan Africa. It is not required if you arrive directly from Europe, North America or Asia.

travelInsurance.text: Travel insurance is not checked at the border, but medical care outside Managua is limited and evacuation is expensive — cover including repatriation is strongly advised.

onwardTicket.text: A confirmed onward or return ticket is expected, and airlines check it at check-in. Overland travelers should be ready to explain their exit plans.

proofOfFunds.text: Officers may ask visitors to show sufficient funds for the stay. A figure of around USD 500, or a credit card, is commonly cited. No amount is formally published, so treat this as guidance rather than a fixed rule.

declarations.text: A paper immigration and customs declaration is handed out on arriving flights and at land borders. Complete it before reaching the counter. The tourist card is bought at the same time.

notes: Fresh food, plants and animal products are restricted. Declare anything agricultural.
Drones and professional camera or broadcast equipment can be held at customs; carry documentation showing it is for personal use.
Drug offenses carry long prison sentences, and border searches at land crossings are thorough.

payments.text: Cards work in Managua, Granada, León and larger hotels, but córdoba cash rules everywhere else — markets, buses, Ometepe and the Caribbean coast. US dollars are widely accepted, though torn or heavily marked notes are refused.

safety.text: Violent crime against tourists is uncommon by regional standards, but the political situation since 2018 has made Nicaragua unpredictable: protests are banned, police may stop and question foreigners, and travelers have been denied entry or expelled over social-media posts or NGO links. Several governments advise reconsidering non-essential travel.

source.name: U.S. Department of State — Nicaragua Travel Advisory

bestTimeToVisit.text: December to April is the dry season — reliable weather for the volcanoes, Granada and the Pacific surf coast. The Caribbean side is wetter year-round and best around March and April.

tips.text: The USD 10 tourist card must be paid in cash in US dollars at the border. Cards are not reliably accepted and there is no ATM before immigration. Carry clean, untorn small notes.

Nicaragua is part of the CA-4 zone with El Salvador, Guatemala and Honduras. Your 90-day allowance is shared across all four countries — crossing between them does not reset the clock, and overstaying incurs a fine on exit.

Immigration screening is political as well as procedural. Journalists, researchers, aid workers and travelers with visible activism on their phones or social media have been refused entry without explanation. Carry hotel bookings and a plain tourist itinerary.

The Peñas Blancas crossing with Costa Rica and Guasaule with Honduras can take two to three hours at peak times. Cross early in the day and keep your tourist card receipt. You may be asked for it on departure.
Nicaragua sits on an active volcanic chain and in the hurricane belt. Check ash advisories for Masaya and Telica, and expect Caribbean-coast disruption between June and November.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for Nicaragua?
faq.answer: Probably not. Nicaragua's Category A covers most of Europe, the Americas, Japan, South Korea, Australia, New Zealand, South Africa and the Gulf states. Those passports need no visa and simply buy a USD 10 tourist card on arrival, valid for up to 90 days. Category B nationalities apply for a consular visa at a Nicaraguan embassy, and Category C nationalities need a "consulted" visa approved in advance by immigration in Managua. Salvadoran, Guatemalan and Honduran citizens move freely under CA-4.

faq.question: What is the Nicaraguan tourist card and how much does it cost?
faq.answer: It is a USD 10 entry card, not a visa. Every visa-exempt visitor buys one in cash at the airport or land border, and it covers a stay of up to 90 days. Keep the receipt — border officers sometimes ask for it when you leave.

faq.question: How long can I stay in Nicaragua?
faq.answer: Visa-exempt visitors are normally granted up to 90 days, and that allowance is shared with El Salvador, Guatemala and Honduras under the CA-4 agreement. An extension of up to a further 90 days can be requested from the Dirección General de Migración y Extranjería in Managua before your stamp expires.

faq.question: How does the CA-4 agreement affect my trip?
faq.answer: El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras and Nicaragua form a single free-movement zone for their own citizens and a single 90-day clock for visitors. Hopping between the four countries does not give you a fresh 90 days. You need to leave the CA-4 area entirely, for example to Costa Rica or Belize.

faq.question: What is a "consulted" visa (visa consultada)?
faq.answer: It is the Category C route used for a restricted list of nationalities. The consulate cannot decide on its own: the application is sent to immigration headquarters in Managua for prior authorization, which typically takes several weeks and often requires a sponsor in Nicaragua. Apply well ahead and confirm current requirements with the nearest Nicaraguan consulate.

faq.question: Is Nicaragua safe to visit right now?
faq.answer: Ordinary crime levels are moderate for the region, but the political environment is the real risk: demonstrations are prohibited, foreigners have been denied entry or expelled, and consular assistance is limited. Check your government's current travel advice before booking and avoid political activity of any kind while in the country.
